source.title: Building Helpful-Only Large Language Models: A Complete Approach from Motivation to Evaluation
source.authors: Donghyeon Ko; Sohee Yang; Donghyun Kwak; Sang-Woo Lee

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether ordinary instruction/preference tuning can change refusal behavior, using refusal-rate evaluations rather than the original study’s fine-tuning setup. Its purpose-built refusal-avoidant training results are not evidence for incidental erosion under ordinary data.
record.gate_note: The paper reports refusal-rate reductions for RAIL, but RAIL explicitly filters refusal examples and adds refusal responses as rejected examples to train refusal avoidance; those induced outcomes are not evidence for the claim about safety erosion from ordinary fine-tuning. The claim-relevant result retained is the authors’ explicit report that unmodified UltraFeedback preference tuning substantially reduces refusal rate. The paper does not test token-position KL, prefilling, suffixes, decoding changes, parameter localization, or safety deepening.
record.test_reason: The study's main method (RAIL) deliberately trains away refusals, so it is not evidence for any version. Two incidental results do bear on the claim, both on a Llama-3.1-8B base given its refusals by WildChat SFT in the same pipeline. First, unmodified UltraFeedback DPO, ordinary preference data, lowers refusal on harmful prompts (V2). Second, the reproduced Shadow-Alignment harmful fine-tuning baseline cuts refusal on harmful prompts sharply (V1). Per-benchmark numbers are in Table 5. This is a new setting, not the originals' recipe, so T3 rather than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude RAIL yields a helpful-only model with 15.06% refusal, a 71.59% reduction vs ALLM and 30.28% vs the attacked LLM, without hurting general capability; it also scores best on HELP. They add that unmodified UltraFeedback already discourages refusal, though this has limited impact on the filtered-SFT model. They report a −0.93 correlation between refusal rate and HELP accuracy. They also find Shadow-Alignment removes refusals but degrades capability and factual accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes RAIL, using refusal filtering, refusal augmentation, SFT, and DPO on WildChat and UltraFeedback; it is not a reproduction of the original few-example fine-tuning method.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that Refusal Filter and Refusal Augmentation have different effects: filtering substantially reduces refusal rates, while augmentation adds a smaller reduction. Refusal-rate outcomes also differ across benchmark sources, as broken down in Appendix G.

fits_no_version.finding: After Shadow-Alignment, the most frequent opening words on benign Arena-Hard prompts change completely ('There are' 189 times), while HOLLM and ALLM openings overlap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful fine-tuning shifts the distribution of response openings even on benign prompts.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 14th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing and the 4th Conference of the Asia-Pacific Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (IJCNLP-AACL), 2025
record.problems: The refusal-rate evaluation uses a prompt-based GPT-4o classifier; the paper notes its evaluation classifier differs from the training classifier, but does not report uncertainty intervals for the refusal-rate effects. The ordinary-data comparison is described qualitatively in the prose, and the flattened tables do not support a confident numeric SFT-to-ALLM assignment. The paper’s main RAIL results are deliberately induced refusal avoidance and therefore do not establish incidental erosion under ordinary fine-tuning.
record.rows_left_out: RAIL refusal-rate outcomes and its filter/augmentation ablations (Sections 6.2 and Appendix G) are left out as claim-version rows because those interventions explicitly train refusal avoidance. The Shadow-Alignment attack result is also not included as a claim-version row: it is an attack deliberately intended to subvert alignment, not a test of the stated opening-token bypass mechanisms. No other study results test V1 or V3–V7.

untested.parts: The number of harmful examples is not stated in this text. Only one attack (Shadow-Alignment) on one 8B model is tested, and no compliance-rate judge beyond refusal classification is used.
No post-release fine-tuning of an established safety-aligned model. No variation in benign-example quantity and no carefully selected benign subsets. Only one model and one dataset (UltraFeedback).
Not tested; no per-token KL measurement.
Not tested; no prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
Not tested. The paper notes UltraFeedback's rejected responses are refusals more often than its chosen ones, but this is offered as a cause of refusal reduction, not of shallowness.

missing.what: Shadow-Alignment harmful fine-tuning vs ALLM, refusal on harmful subsets: AdvBench 90.19→19.81, SORRY 63.56→26.00, XSTest unsafe 92.00→29.00, OR-Bench toxic 76.64→14.81; overall 53.01→21.60. Capability costs are in Table 1. This was wrongly excluded: harmful fine-tuning is exactly what V1 names.
missing.locator: Section 5.2.1, Section 6.2, Table 1, Table 5 (Attacked LLM row)

missing.what: UltraFeedback DPO on the refusal-filtered SFT model leaves refusal unchanged: overall 28.76→29.70, AdvBench 39.42→39.62, SORRY 33.11→32.67, OR-Bench toxic 29.77→32.82.

record.verdict_notes: RAIL results are correctly excluded as deliberately induced refusal removal. Refusal rate is judged by a prompted GPT-4o classifier, with no uncertainty reported. Totals mix harmful and seemingly-harmful prompts, so harmful subsets should be used for V1/V2. The 'aligned' model is a pipeline-built SFT model, not a released safety-tuned chat model. The number of Shadow-Alignment examples is not given in this text.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred harmful examples and no test of harmful-example-induced compliance.

Tests unmodified instruction/preference datasets, not a controlled comparison of benign-example quantities or carefully selected benign subsets; the text does not establish a few-to-hundreds-example effect.
No per-token KL or response-position measurement.
No compliant-opening prefill, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change test. The reported fine-tuning-based attack is designed to subvert alignment and is not a test of those bypass mechanisms.
No weight or rank localization experiment.
No test of why safety would be shallow or of the data/objective producing shallowness.
No training designed to spread safety across response positions or test of whether such training holds up.

rows.subject: ALLM (Llama-3.1-8B trained on unprocessed datasets)
rows.stage_stated: instruction tuned with unprocessed datasets: WildChat SFT and UltraFeedback RL
rows.operation_detail: Unmodified UltraFeedback preference tuning; the paper reports that this substantially reduces refusal rate relative to the preceding SFT model.

conditions.value: UltraFeedback without Refusal Filter or Refusal Augmentation
refusal-rate evaluation on the paper’s refusal-avoidance benchmarks

rows.baseline: preceding SFT model trained on WildChat; numeric baseline not stated in the prose
rows.value: The authors state that unmodified UltraFeedback RL leads to a substantial reduction in refusal rate; exact comparison value not stated in the prose.
rows.note: The paper attributes the effect partly to UltraFeedback’s existing preference structure: rejected responses classified as refusals outnumber chosen responses classified as refusals by more than two to one (Table 2). This is an ordinary-data training result, not the explicitly refusal-avoidant RAIL intervention. The flattened tables do not make a numeric SFT-to-ALLM comparison safe to assign to this row.
rows.check: Value and baseline can be read from Tables 1 and 5; they are not missing. Overall refusal falls 70.95 (SFT on D_SFT) to 53.01 (ALLM), but that total mixes in over-refusal prompts. On harmful subsets: AdvBench 97.12→90.19, SORRY 76.89→63.56, XSTest unsafe 99.00→92.00, OR-Bench toxic 94.81→76.64. These are 7–18 point drops with refusal still high, so partial. Subject caveat: the model is not a prior safety-trained release; its refusals come from WildChat SFT in the same pipeline.

relationships.condition: Unmodified UltraFeedback DPO applied to Llama-3.1-8B after WildChat SFT (unfiltered SFT data)
relationships.reason: Refusal on harmful prompts drops on every harmful subset, e.g. SORRY 76.89→63.56 and OR-Bench toxic 94.81→76.64 (Table 5). The drop is moderate, and the starting refusals come from in-pipeline SFT (r1).
relationships.display_finding: Refusal on harmful prompts fell on every harmful subset, for example SORRY from 76.89 to 63.56 and OR-Bench toxic from 94.81 to 76.64, a moderate drop from refusal levels set by the earlier SFT stage.
